title: Man killed by police in Nova Scotia had ties to Moncton
article: A 22-year-old man who was shot and killed by police in Nova Scotia earlier this month is being remembered by a family friend for his kind heart and unreached potential.

While the RCMP would not confirm the identity ot the man, Felix Cacchione, director of the Nova Scotia Serious Incident Response Team, which is investigating the shooting, confirmed it was Mitchell Speight.

Cheryl Allen, an Amherst resident who said she has known Speight since he was about 10 years old, said over the years he split his time between Moncton and Amherst, N.S., and also spent some time living in Miramichi.
Speight and her son became close friends growing up after she and her family relocated from Calgary, she said.

"Mitchell was a source of sanity for my son - he took him under his wing, welcomed him with open arms, they played golf, hockey and soccer together," said Allen. "Mitchell was a gifted athlete and a brilliant kid, the kindest heart you'll ever see. He had so much potential."
But things started "deteriorating" after his mother died in 2010, when Speight was 13 years old, she said.
"When his mom passed, it was traumatic. He and his mom were very close. She was his soft place to land," said Allen, who spoke with the Times & Transcript with the consent of a family member.
Speight's obituary reads that he will be remembered for his "sensitive and loving nature, his ability to lift others up with his sense of humour and his beautiful smile."
It states he was a gifted athlete who participated in school athletics and provincial teams in hockey, soccer and golf. Mitchell was also an honour student, his obituary says.

In 2017, Speight was found guilty of multiple charges, including possession of property obtained by crime, breach of probation/curfew, theft of motor vehicle and possession of cannabis, according to court documents obtained by the Times & Transcript.

On May 15, he was sentenced to 85 days in jail, said Jennifer Stairs, a spokesperson for the Executive Office of the Nova Scotia Judiciary, adding charges included dangerous operation of a motor vehicle.

Events leading to his death on Aug. 10 started when RCMP members were investigating a complaint of a stolen vehicle that had been spotted in Truro. One officer was struck by the suspect vehicle and then fired their service pistol at the driver, killing the man, RCMP said in a news release.
The officer was injured and taken to hospital with serious but non life-threatening injuries, police said, adding no one else was injured during the incident.
Allen, who saw Speight for the last time in February, when she gave him a ride from Moncton to Amherst, said if she could have seen his future when he was just a kid, she wouldn't have believed it.
"But when I read that someone was shot in a stolen car, the first thing I did was to reach out to law enforcement and ask if this was Mitchell," she said.

Allen is now hoping to "make something positive" out of Speight's death by creating a support group for youth struggling with the loss of a parent. The support group would pair up teenagers with adults who can offer them emotional stability, she said.

"It's a buddy to take you golfing, play tennis with. If they \[teenagers\] feel comfortable enough, and they want to talk, then they do it. They have a soft place to land. If you can't fix it \[the pain\], you walk beside them, you support them," said Allen.
"That's where I feel we let Mitchell down."
The Times & Transcript also reached out to family members, but they either did not respond or declined to comment.
